steps.title: Brunello di Montalcino
steps.body: Montalcino, a hill town south of Siena, is warmer and drier than Chianti. Brunello di Montalcino, DOCG since 1980, must be 100% Sangiovese and age at least five years, two in oak, before release; Riserva six years. The Biondi-Santi family created the style in the late 19th century. Rosso di Montalcino is the younger, cheaper version.

steps.title: Vino Nobile
steps.body: Montepulciano, east of Montalcino, makes Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG from at least 70% Sangiovese, locally called Prugnolo Gentile. It ages at least two years. It's often softer than Brunello and more structured than Chianti. Not to be confused with Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, a different grape and region.

steps.prompt: What does Brunello di Montalcino require?
steps.explanation: Brunello is pure Sangiovese, aged at least five years before release.

steps.title: Comparing
steps.body: Chianti Classico is often the freshest, with sour cherry and violet. Brunello, from a warmer place and with longer ageing, is fuller, more powerful and long-lived. Vino Nobile sits between them. All three show Sangiovese's acidity and tannin.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its rule.
steps.explanation: Each Tuscan wine sets its own rules.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Brunello is 100% Sangiovese, aged five years
Vino Nobile is at least 70% Prugnolo Gentile
Brunello is fullest; Chianti Classico freshest
